title: Google makes big plans for wallet
snippet: The tech giant envisions its digital wallet assuming a larger role in commerce than merely point-of-sale payments, Google’s payments head said.
fullText:
For many consumers, the digital wallet is their home for payment cards, and maybe an ID. 

Google has a far grander vision of what its wallet should be and do, including a repository for receipts, tracking online orders, arranging refunds and transmitting merchant discounts and other marketing promotions, the technology company’s head of payments said last week in an interview.

Adding new capabilities to Google’s wallet will boost adoption and offer consumers a more “seamless” retail experience, said Stavan Parikh, vice president and general manager of payments at the company.

A more robust digital wallet will mean “that you can truly start leaving your home without your physical wallet,” he said Oct. 26. “So far, most of us can’t do it because there's always one thing that we need to carry.”

That reliance on the physical wallet will begin to change as people find they can use their digital wallet for more than a payment or to store their loyalty cards, he said.

The wallet push gives Google “an opportunity to make commerce journeys more seamless, both across online and offline, because the vast majority of commerce today still happens offline, and the offline journey hasn’t yet been enhanced with digital wallets or technology in some of these ways,” Parikh said.

Over the past few months, Google has redesigned multiple aspects of its Android-based wallet. Among some of the more prominent changes are an expanded form autofill capacity for the Chrome browser with a closer integration to the wallet, announced in June. Google is also tweaking the wallet to allow for larger images and more space for brands.

Shopping bargains delivered via the wallet will be a crucial path to further digitize the retail world and drive further wallet use, Parikh said, as people seek to save money and simplify their transactions.

“Saving money is a higher-order” priority for consumers, he said. “A lot of commerce transactions are tied to that, and we are partnering with merchants. We are partnering with the (Google) shopping team and others to kind of say, ‘How do we connect the dots so that the right offer shows up to the user at the right time?’”

The tech world is also leading the push into agentic commerce, with companies from OpenAI to Google, as well as card networks Mastercard and Visa and digital payments company Stripe, all advancing technical protocols and other efforts to bring shopping to artificial intelligence agents.

Digital wallets are likely to assume more importance in the arena of agentic commerce as the means for digital agents to pay for goods and services on behalf of humans, Lisa Yokoyama, a director of product management for Google Pay, said during an Oct. 20 panel discussion of agentic commerce at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas. 

Stripe, for example, is promoting its Link wallet as an agentic payment tool, working with Meta Platforms and other agent purveyors.

A digital wallet offers merchants and consumers a “more immersive, more interactive surface where card art can be vibrant and visual,” Yokoyama said during the agentic commerce discussion.

“Transactions can be done in real-time on a surface that's in context of the exact transaction or the online checkout flow,” she said. “That created a dialog in a way that you can’t with an analog piece of plastic or metal.”

Google also wants to leverage agentic commerce with infrastructure that would allow people to give a third-party agent “a credential that is constrained in some way and doesn’t leak your private information that you may not want to leak,” he said.

“That's what we have done with Gemini and (Google) Pay … to give these agents credentials that are constrained and ensure that users can continue trusting it,” Parikh said. “The opportunity is definitely there, and I think the infrastructure is there. Now, can we get the right product experience out? (That) is the piece that we are focused on.”

Over time, Parikh sees the wallet becoming a more helpful consumer tool tied closer to the entire shopping experience than how most people use them today.

Beyond a payment, wallets should also allow users to see the status of the transaction, react to a transaction and handle refunds, with “all of those things in your digital wallet,” he said. “We're really just kind of scaling the wallet for end-to-end commercial journeys.”

fullText:
Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House.

  

Speaker: Nikhil Rathi, chief executive 

Event: Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner 

Delivered: 22 October 2026 

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Highlights

The UK’s financial services strength provides a platform to lead the next era of technology-driven growth. 

We must move faster and focus on outcomes to protect market integrity without holding back innovation. 

The FCA will make better use of technology and intelligence and more assertive use of its powers to tackle system-wide risks and financial crime. 

Stronger partnerships between regulators, industry, government and others is essential to protect market integrity.

    

            						

The success of the UK’s financial services

In August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston.   

A Red Sox game, perhaps? No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.

Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life. Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.

Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.

It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.

On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters. Yet there’s plenty to cheer.

We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…

A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of…  

Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.

UK firms leading in:

artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.

consumer access to investment opportunities widened.

moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.

Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City. Thank you for your leadership.

If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

          

            						

I say 'we' because the FCA plays an important role.

Financial services businesses and investors need confidence in markets…including their ability to withstand and recover from shocks.

That’s why ensuring the integrity of the financial services system is an FCA primary objective.

Tonight, I want to explain how we maintain it as technology accelerates exponentially. Because, while we may be getting past peak rule making, we are nowhere near peak reform or innovation. Nor past the peak intervention required to disrupt harm and support market integrity and growth.

We have seen radical technological change before… But never so widespread or disruptive. Nor combined, as now, with a new geopolitical and defence order.

The trouble is our system responds too slowly. And trust in institutions is eroded if we can’t solve problems quickly.

Regulation takes time. Legislation requires scrutiny. Parliamentary resource is precious.

Our judicial system is under immense pressure, with more litigation and weightier decisions. We risk delays becoming the norm, with legal claims written with AI’s help potentially making things worse.

We all play a part in a system that prioritises safety in process over ruthless focus on outcomes and delivery.

So, the UK finds itself in a dangerous 'innovation delta': where institutions tasked with regulating markets and the mechanisms holding us accountable lag behind.

If we maintain an analogue approach in a digital age, new products enter the market faster than we adapt… Leaving us reacting to, even overwhelmed by, changes rather than shaping conditions for the UK to thrive.

Take Meta Muse, launched 6 weeks ago, one of the fastest-downloaded apps in US history. Personal agents are profoundly changing how consumers interact with financial and health services. Such applications will reach UK consumers soon.

Frontier AI models are here, making it easier for AI agents to carry out tasks increasingly autonomously. You are fast adopters.

And rapid change in wholesale markets:

decentralised finance

24/7 trading a reality with prices increasingly forming over weekends

parallel market structures operating alongside traditional ones

Vast opportunities. But the threats to market integrity are as serious as I have seen them.

Unprecedented volatility, concentration risks, new forms of market abuse and rampant cross-border financial crime: fast-emerging technologies putting these on steroids.

Cyber security too mixes the frailties of human nature and high tech.

Our own AI minister recently said it was likely that at some point the UK’s systems will be breached. Which is why reporting and learning from near misses is so important. As is insurance for you, your customers and supply chain.

Prevention will not always work, so investment in recovery is a necessity. The gravity of the decision to press a kill switch may pale in significance with the enormity of the task to get a system running again.

In the face of all today’s challenges, the temptation is to say: 'write more rules, but do it damned well faster'.

We will, where we need to… Including aligning with any national or global AI standards, which the Prime Minister has said will be a focus of the UK’s upcoming G20 presidency.

But if policymaking is our only regulatory reflex, we’ll be stuck chasing yesterday’s market instead of embracing the one in front of us.

          

            						

Regulatory reform continues

I do not mean to suggest that we will slow down rule reform or modernisation. But our focus must be on outcomes.

We have reformed our rulebook and strengthened our operations. Capital market reforms have kicked in. 

Technology is making it easier to interact with us with reduced reporting burdens. Our widest ever range of innovation services with record demand.

And we promised less intensive supervision for those clearly trying to do the right thing, so we can focus where harm is greatest.

But the impact won’t be fully felt unless we also end tickbox compliance. Reams of potentially duplicative assurance – data packs, risk reports, internal audit. Some of these processes driven by commercial choice, others by regulation and legislation.

Sarah Pritchard, the FCA’s deputy chief executive, will engage with you to streamline unnecessary effort…. To give Boards confidence to be brave. And consider if it’s time to look again at the 3 lines of defence.

As much as 8% of banks’ workforces are dedicated to combatting crime. We should be delivering far better outcomes with those resources.

Yet we’re bogged down by excessive data collection, complex validation, and a limited ability to understand a customer’s wider context and identify risks that span borders, institutions and accounts…

As we integrate over 60,000 professional services businesses into our ambit, Johan Sekora, our new chief operating officer, who previously led Swedish banks' intelligence sharing efforts, will spearhead work to look beyond know your customer (KYC) process so we unearth actual money laundering.

Information collected through KYC, transaction and sanctions monitoring will remain valuable.

We are ready to experiment, so we can focus collective resources exactly where they are needed….

Within the FCA, too, we must continue to get better at joining up the dots. AI tools give our supervisors a richer risk picture…

…Agents can assess cases, synthesise returns and intelligence… parse millions of rows of data and identify missing or concerning information…

Freeing up our people to do the work we need experts to do: to make the hardest decisions… Such as when agentic coordination becomes market manipulation. Or judging when a risk becomes system-wide.

Expanded capability means we’ll find more risks. So, we’ll need to be open about which justify the use of resources and which don’t.

          

            						

Powers and partnership

As an institution, we have not always persuaded others of the need for legislative change… And even when we have, change has been welcome but often slow.

So: how can we do our job effectively when technology advances faster than we can write laws or rules?

The answer must be to rethink how we use powers we already have.

We have system-wide responsibilities, but a fixed view of who we explicitly regulate.

Government and Parliament decide who we authorise. This perimeter is our anchor. But we cannot let it weigh so heavily that it sinks the regulatory ship.

Today’s risks aren’t polite enough to knock on our door to introduce themselves.

Market, cyber, or criminal risks emerge from multiple networks, firms and jurisdictions….

Capital flows across sectors, regulated or not, creating complex webs of commercial incentives. And harms within our remit originating outside it. Be that mass digital harm on social media.

Insider trading on offshore gambling or prediction markets. Or outages – like Google Cloud this week – disrupting people’s access to vital services. Talk of such system-wide risks is far from academic.

Money laundering through the regulated system is not just about fraud, sanctions and tax evasion, it funds human and drugs trafficking. Their victims: society’s most vulnerable.

Parliament has provided tools to deal with such system-wide issues affecting our objectives and remit:

The Enterprise, Consumer Rights and Online Safety and Digital Market Acts to name 4.

The critical third-parties regime. An expanding anti-money-laundering remit.

It isn’t enough to ask: is this in our perimeter?

If significant harm affects markets within our remit, we should ask: what powers do we have to tackle it? Would this be a good use of resources?

The same is true of growth opportunities. Not what are they, but how can we enable them?

In every instance: who can we work with to make a difference, quickly? Because no single agency can rise to today’s challenges alone.

Working with the Met, National Crime Agency and HMRC, we’ve recently undertaken 2 of our most significant operations to disrupt suspected organised criminal gangs who seek to abuse our financial system.

So, effective partnerships are already in action:

Cooperation through the Digital Regulators Forum on Meta Muse.

A big delivery year for pensions with the Pensions Regulator and DWP.

A FCA-Bank of England roadmap on digital assets soon dovetailing with the work Chris Woolard and the industry have been doing.

And work with international counterparts.

Recent action by US authorities against anti-money laundering violations confirming the fight against financial crime remains global. 

          

            						

Call to action: we need you

We should also be open to ideas about how we can act at pace and scale.

We have seen dedicated financial services courts speed things up in other markets, for example… And the accountability system could foster collaborative working.

There are significant mechanisms to hold the FCA accountable, more than for most regulators. Appropriate given the significance of our work and the breadth of powers entrusted to us.

But accountability must be system-wide too. Whether that is to press hard on growth or engage on risks, and which are priorities and which aren’t.

Parliament is the only body that can ensure accountability across rather than within narrow remits, transcending traditional committee boundaries.

And as we significantly step up the intensity of our activity to address system-wide risks, we need you.

The earlier we can work with you – the firms we regulate and civil society – to identify emerging risks and opportunities, the faster we can give you the confidence to move.

          

            						

Close: the prize

In other words, partnership.

That is what we need now. Partnership not just between financial regulators but more widely.

Only through partnership can we deliver the system-wide response needed to protect market integrity. And that is the foundation necessary so innovation can flourish, productivity can rise and growth can endure.

The UK is incredibly well placed to harness the power of new technology. The existing strength of this sector gives us a genuine head start.

If we can harness technological progress – if we continue to lead – financial services can place the UK at the forefront of this new era of innovation.

As regulators, we are committed to creating the conditions for you to do that.

Together, we can build a future that the whole country will be proud of…

title: Bilt tackles sports with $300M deal
snippet: The rent-rewards startup aims to stretch beyond housing payments and credit cards by buying Lava, a technology firm that focuses on sports loyalty.
fullText:
Bilt Technologies, a fintech best known for letting its users earn reward points in exchange for charging their rent to a credit card, has agreed to acquire the sports loyalty technology firm Lava in a $300 million deal, the companies said Monday.

“Sports have an extraordinary ability to bring people together, yet the relationship between teams, fans and their neighborhoods has barely been tapped,” Bilt founder and CEO Ankur Jain said in a statement. “Lava has built incredible technology connecting sports organizations with their fans. Bringing that together with Bilt opens up an entirely new frontier for what membership and loyalty can mean.”

Lava’s platform harnesses more than 300 technology adapters connecting point-of-sale, identity, loyalty, ticketing and payments – through which sports teams and entertainment venues can recognize customers, cater personalized benefits, manage loyalty programs and partner in real-time experiences, the company said. 

It boasts relationships with 56 professional sports franchises, including the NFL’s Detroit Lions, NBA’s Denver Nuggets and NHL’s Carolina Hurricanes.

“Teams have built extraordinary loyalty, and Bilt brings the network to make that loyalty valuable across everyday life,” said Lava co-founder Vivek Ranadivé, who also owns the NBA’s Sacramento Kings. “Lava joining Bilt will help our partners turn sports fandom into a neighborhood economy that works for fans, teams and local businesses every day.”

With the deal, Bilt aims to combine its artificial intelligence agents with Lava’s real-time engagement technology to create personalized benefits through local businesses, based on a web of shared data points.

Bilt, for its part, touts about 7 million members in its network of residential communities, and partnerships with about 50,000 merchants.

The Lava deal may also represent a pivot that allows Bilt to move past a public breakup with one of its largest partners, Wells Fargo.

The bank last year decided to cut short a credit-card partnership with Bilt over concerns that the tie-up was losing money, according to The Wall Street Journal. The partnership was initially slated to run through 2029, but the fracture gained even more notoriety when new credit cards were issued to dozens of customers who opted to close their accounts – just ahead of the alliance’s end.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered Bilt in June to reimburse roughly 500 customers for fees charged amid the company’s transition to a new bank partner.

Wen Miao, Lava’s CEO and co-founder, said he’s excited for the chance to take his company’s technology past the confines of the sports venue.

“Loyalty shouldn’t begin and end on game day,” Miao said Monday. “Together, we have an opportunity to redefine how loyalty works, not just on game day, but throughout everyday life.”

title: UK Adults Want Tax Cuts but not the Spending Cuts to Pay for Them
snippet: Taxd research finds 58 per cent of UK adults would cut council tax and half would cut VAT, but only a third would accept lower public spending to pay for it. The post UK Adults Want Tax Cuts but not the Spending Cuts to Pay for Them appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
British adults want relief on council tax and VAT, but most are unwilling to accept lower spending on public services to fund it, according to new research from tax filing platform Taxd.

Taxd‘s If I Were In Charge report asked a simple question: if you ran the Treasury, what would you change? Nearly six in ten adults (58 per cent) said they would cut council tax, against just 7 per cent who would raise it. Half (50 per cent) would cut VAT. Yet only a third (33 per cent) said they would cut taxes if it meant spending less on public services.

That gap leaves the Chancellor with a harder choice than the familiar argument over whether taxes should rise or fall, with the Budget approaching and household finances under scrutiny.

A question of fairness

Arjun Kumar, co-CEO and co-founder of Taxd

The research also points to a sense of unfairness. Some 56 per cent of respondents said the tax system is unfair to people like them, compared with 18 per cent who said it is fair. Among those who feel it is unfair, 43 per cent said tax rises had not been matched by better public services.

The findings are not simple anti-tax sentiment, however. Many respondents said they would be willing to pay more if they could see where the money goes.

Arjun Kumar, co-founder and co-CEO of Taxd, said: “What comes through is not a demand for simply more or less tax, but for a different shape of taxation: lighter on work and everyday spending, and more willing to look at wealth.”

“The same answers show the bind any Chancellor is in. Nearly six in ten adults would cut council tax and half would cut VAT, but only a third would accept lower public spending to pay for it. Every pound taken off one tax has to be found somewhere else, and an honest debate has to start there.”

Kumar is a former tax director at PwC who left to build Taxd, an HMRC-recognised self-assessment filing platform that supports more than 20,000 users.

The core data comes from a nationally representative Opinium poll of 2,050 UK adults, conducted between 9 and 11 September 2026, supported by 1,173 open responses gathered through Taxd’s public microsite.

title: Mastercard scales in India
snippet: The card network expanded its tie with the country’s largest private bank, increasing its opportunities to sell to small businesses and consumers.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                

The card network expanded its tie with the country’s largest private bank, increasing its opportunities to sell to small businesses and consumers.

        

            

        Published Nov. 2, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Shoppers buy onions from a street stall at Boro Bazar on March 19, 2026, in Dhubri, Assam, India. Mastercard has been seeking to expand its reach in the country.
            
        
            Getty Images News via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Mastercard has expanded its work with the largest bank in India, the world’s most populous country, according to comments from the card network’s CEO, Michael Miebach.

In reporting the company’s third-quarter results last week, Miebach said Mastercard had signed a small business-focused agreement with HDFC Bank during the quarter, giving the network an opportunity to sell services to the bank and potentially offer another three million cards. 

Mastercard has had a relationship with the bank since 2005, a spokesperson for the card network said by email. The company’s larger U.S. rival, Visa also has a tie to HDFC. 

The Indian bank has some 10,000 branch locations and provides services to 100 million customers, Miebach said Thursday on an earnings call.

Miebach called the business expansion an “important” development in “one of the world's most competitive markets.”

The expanded partnership comes as the Purchase, New York-based company to further its build its presence in countries around the world and increase its global market share. 

Miebach noted that the card network is cultivating relationships to reach unbanked customers in African countries like Nigeria, to cater to wealthy clients in Switzerland and to build ties in India and Brazil, where those nations’ governments have created national payment systems.

Miebach explained how the Indian government creating the UPI payment system to include more people in the country’s financial system is both a challenge to companies offering services in that country and an opportunity.

He noted news reports since August that UPI may begin to charge merchants a fee to help finance the national payments system.

“We continue to engage in India very effectively with the government, (and) with the private sector,” Miebach said, strengthening Mastercard’s debit card proposition to better compete in the market. 

UPI is bringing people “into the digital ecosystem that will graduate to different sets of products, which will include debit, and then eventually credit,” Miebach said. “There is so much opportunity in India as well as in Brazil, where we essentially pursue the same strategy.”

In both countries, Mastercard partners with companies and governments, he explained.

The company’s third-quarter U.S. gross dollar volume rose 6% over the year-earlier period to $867 billion, but a faster 8% rate to a larger $2.08 trillion outside of the U.S., according to the third-quarter presentation. Based on that third-quarter view, the business outside the U.S. makes up about 70% of the company’s volume.

Third-quarter net income climbed 18% over the year-ago period to $4.6 billion as revenue for the quarter increased 14% to $9.8 billion, according to the company’s earnings press release.

fullText:
The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.

Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.

Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.

Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.

But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.

Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.

That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.

The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusion

The current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.

The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.

But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.

The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.

That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.

Defence is not one-size-fits-all

There is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.

One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.

The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.

Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.

A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.

Better information leads to better decisions

Another theme that stood out was the importance of data.

Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.

Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:

Are applications taking longer than expected?

Are decisions being applied consistently?

Do governance processes reflect actual risk?

Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?

Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.

Getting the balance right

Our work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.

When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.

Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.

title: T+1 is a Year away and a Quarter of Firms Still have no Plan
snippet: With T+1 about a year away, Aqua Global finds 23 per cent of financial institutions have no plan, and CEO Cian Fernando warns of rushed, costly overhauls. The post T+1 is a Year away and a Quarter of Firms Still have no Plan appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
With the move to T+1 settlement about a year away, nearly a quarter of financial institutions still have no plan in place to meet the deadline, according to research from Aqua Global Solutions.

Aqua Global’s research found that 23 per cent of financial institutions have yet to put plans in place for the shorter settlement cycle, which takes effect on 11 October 2027. The transition cuts the time between a trade and its settlement to one business day, leaving far less room for manual processing and exception handling.

Cian Fernando, CEO of Aqua Global, warned that the remaining time is barely enough for banks still dependent on legacy systems, and that those who leave it late face costly overhauls.

“Readiness across the industry remains patchy. Many banks still run on legacy infrastructure that simply can’t settle trades fast enough. If they don’t modernise soon, they’ll face failed settlements, cash penalties, funding pressure and operational strain,” he said.

Late movers pay more

For Fernando, the risk lies less in the date itself than in delay. Banks that are slow to move from manual intervention to automated handling, he argued, will end up in rushed transformation programmes, reworking core processes under time pressure and regulatory scrutiny as costs and risk build.

“A year can feel like a long time. But the real pressure isn’t the deadline, it’s leaving preparations too late,” he said.

He also framed the change as an opportunity rather than only a compliance exercise. Faster settlement reduces counterparty exposure and market risk, and the automation needed to achieve it allows firms to handle higher volumes without adding headcount.

“Banks that move now will gain an edge. T+1 isn’t just a regulatory requirement, but a genuine opportunity to innovate,” Fernando said. “Early movers will be operating with confidence while their competitors are still firefighting.”

title: Truist bolsters merchant tools
snippet: The super-regional rolled out a faster onboarding experience and added insights for business owners, said Chris Ward, head of enterprise payments.
fullText:
Truist is boosting its services for merchant clients, rolling out a faster onboarding experience, new management capabilities and an enhanced view of payment activity, the company said Tuesday. 

The Charlotte, North Carolina-based bank is buttressing its business management tools with an assist from Fiserv’s Clover point-of-sale system and Early Warning Services’ Paze digital wallet as an online checkout option, according to a press release on the expanded services. 

There’s “a larger opportunity for us to make this more relevant to our clients' day-to-day operation,” said Chris Ward, who is head of enterprise payments for the bank.

The enhancements are designed to strengthen the entire experience for Truist’s merchant clients, Ward said. All new features are live, after being piloted last quarter, he said; more tweaks are in the works, although he declined to share details. 

The crowded merchant acquiring segment has gone beyond payment processing to include software and other value-added services in recent years. Merchant services is a “big, important part” of Truist “becoming more critical” to clients’ payment needs, Ward said. 

Rather than offering point solutions, “we’ve done a nice job of integrating a set of capabilities together, so it’s not just one piece, it’s bringing multiple things together, and I think that gives us a differentiated experience,” he said.

The merchant segment can also serve as the connection point to other areas of the bank, including deposits, treasury and lending, as Truist helps clients consider cash flow, liquidity and capital needs, Ward said. 

Truist doesn’t disclose the size of the merchant services business, but it’s one where executives “see meaningful opportunity for growth,” Ward said. The bank reported card and treasury management fees rose 2% year over year, to $347 million, in the third quarter.

During Mike Lyons’ first earnings call as CEO of $554 billion-asset Truist, he mentioned growth opportunities in payments, including expanding the bank’s consumer credit card business and its treasury management business on the wholesale side.

Truist is “focused on closing key gaps” and "building digital and payments capabilities, including mobile banking, treasury management, and credit cards,” Lyons said during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call Oct. 16. 

Ward declined to comment on Lyons’ strategy. However, Ward said he thinks “payments is a critical component to the firm and a critical component to driving primacy for consumers, for small businesses, for wholesale clients,” he said during an interview at last month’s Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. 

Lyons, who briefly served as CEO of Fiserv before taking the helm of Truist, is “a big supporter of payments,” Ward said. “It’s great for our business.”

Truist has had a “long-standing relationship” with Clover, and Tuesday’s announcement represents an expansion of that tie-up, Ward said.  

Ward having oversight of both consumer and wholesale payments at the bank makes for “richer capabilities” for clients in both segments, he said. He’s intent on making payments speedier, simpler, safer and smarter for the bank’s clients.

“I don't think any consumer or business wakes up and says, ‘Oh, I want to make an ACH [payment] today,’” he said. Instead, it’s “‘Hey, I’ve got to pay somebody.’ And that's really how we think about how we should tackle things.”

Payments is a crucial component to becoming a client’s primary bank, and primacy, in turn, is key to the bank’s growth, Ward said. 

The broader shift toward faster, digital payments, particularly in the commercial world where there’s lots of room to run, is also a growth accelerant for the bank, Ward said. “There's still a lot of transactions that still could be card-able in a [business-to-business] context,” he said.

title: AI agents won’t pay the way you do
snippet: Plaid’s payments head explains how payment methods might shift as artificial intelligence begins choosing how to pay.
fullText:
As agentic commerce gains wider use, the payments industry is pondering how artificial intelligence may herald a change in payment methods. 

Bots won’t be bothered by traditional payment frictions that torment humans, such as confusing checkout flows, account creation forms, password setup or poor user interfaces. 

An agent will focus on payment parameters the human consumer has provided, such as maximizing discounts or card-issuer rewards, and select the payment method it views as offering attributes that align with those guidelines, said Brian Dammeir, head of payments and financial management at Plaid. 

The San Francisco-based financial data aggregator transfers consumer account information between banks and fintechs.

As a result, it’s likely that banks, card issuers, merchants and the card networks will see shifts relative to how people pay today, he said. Dammeir discussed Plaid’s payments business and agentic transactions during an Oct. 19 interview on the sidelines of the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity. 

PAYMENTS DIVE: How do you see the payments ecosystem changing if agents, and not humans, select a payment method?

Optional Caption

Permission granted by Plaid

BRIAN DAMMEIR: I think the main thing folks opine on, or think about, and we think a lot about this, is in an agentic world will there be different consumer preferences around payments? If, at the end of the day, you’re permissioning something to an agent, and the agent's incentive is to take the most efficient, or most effective, route to pay for the consumer they’re acting on behalf of, you could certainly see a world in which, for example, bank payments are adopted more broadly, and you could see the mix of payment methods changing in this world. That being said, I think that's all going to depend on the consumer experience and what each of those things looks like to the consumer and which appeals to them more.

Does that lead to a new world of incentives by companies to lure a bot to a particular payment option?

The opportunity here for any network payment method player is that there’s going to be a world now in which agents are talking to agents and making a decision, and representing all parties. I’ll have an agent that represents me as, let’s say, someone buying a shirt. There’s an agent on the other side representing the merchant in their best interest. Whoever is able to create technologies that allows those agents to make the best decision, hypothetically, is going to do better in the end. Now, does that then end up being like the card-centric world, the bank-payment world, or various other payment methods? Only time will tell. But that is the opportunity, right?

Will this payment decision be made at the consumer level, with humans setting those parameters, maybe choosing travel rewards or highest cash-back offers? Or will these selections rest with the agents?

The consumer really does drive behavior. Now, we as payments experts are going to know many of the idiosyncrasies of what’s going on underneath. In the card world, it’s interchange (cost), and maybe there will be these agentic standards and how they’re all talking to each other. Most consumers will not have knowledge of that, but they will understand the value they’re being given. If I tell my agent, I love flying, I love travel, I want to optimize for what’s going to give me the best there. Or maybe I’m someone who just optimizes for cash in my pocket, and I want simplicity. That’s not too dissimilar from the world today, but agents are going to be able to work through that question much more effectively than a consumer has been able to. The agent can be an expert, but the consumer doesn’t have to be. So that is what’s going to shift behavior.

What do you see in terms of agentic payments today?

Most (agents) generally have one or two wallets available. It’s early days. There’s a lot of just initial, ‘Hey, we need to get started, we need some payment methods.’ But I expect a year from now, it’s going to look very different than it does right now. It's going to be a lot more options, including, in our view, paying by bank in certain contexts.

Dive Brief:

U.S. Bank’s Jodi Richard, chief risk officer and a vice chair, has left the Minneapolis-based lender to become chief risk officer of American Express and its national bank, effective Jan. 25, 2027, Amex said in a Thursday memo.

Troy Remington, U.S. Bank’s chief credit officer and an executive vice president, will serve as the lender’s interim risk chief while it searches for a successor, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission filing Thursday.  

Richard, who notified U.S. Bank of her departure Oct. 23, had been at the super-regional since 2014. She was appointed chief risk officer in 2018. At Amex, Richard will also become head of the global risk and compliance team and report to CEO Stephen Squeri.

Dive Insight:

The executive shuffle comes at a pivotal time for Amex, which was hit this month with a $350 million civil penalty and enforcement actions from the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency over anti-money laundering compliance failures.

Given her experience, Richard “understands risk from both a regulatory and business perspective and has spent her career helping companies navigate change and growth while maintaining a strong control environment,” Squeri said in Thursday’s memo. 

“Throughout her career in banking, Jodi has demonstrated that risk management should be an effective partner to the business, and that while the need to innovate and grow is important, what is even more critical is taking the right risks responsibly,” the CEO wrote. “This is imperative to protecting our customers and our company while enabling the business to move forward.”  

In her new role, Richard will be based in New York and join Amex’s executive committee, Squeri said. Amex’s current risk chief, Doug Tabish, will become president of enterprise shared services in February, after the current executive in that role, Denise Pickett, retires, Squeri said in a memo issued Wednesday. 

Richard’s resignation from U.S. Bank “was not due to any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to the Company’s operations, policies or practices,” the SEC filing noted.  

Prior to becoming CRO at U.S. Bank, Richard had been the lender’s chief operational risk officer. Before joining the $703 billion-asset bank, she spent about 11 years at HSBC, where she held roles in risk management and regulatory compliance. 

Richard also spent about 12 years at the OCC, in two separate stints, according to her LinkedIn profile. She was a national bank examiner specializing in retail credit. 

She also served as chief compliance officer for Sears National Bank. 

Remington, meanwhile, has been at U.S. Bank for more than 21 years, according to his LinkedIn profile. He was appointed chief credit officer in 2021.

Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes.

  

            						

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.

Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.

Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.

Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

title: Fiserv talks to potential asset buyers
snippet: The processor has started engaging with potential buyers for the sale of some of its assets, the CEO said. It has also doubled its savings goal to $1 billion.
fullText:
Fiserv is now targeting $1 billion in savings, up from $500 million, as its new CEO seeks to transform the business into one generating more revenue and profits.

In reporting its third-quarter earnings results Tuesday, CEO Takis Georgakopoulos said that a previously announced review of the company’s operations and technology had allowed it to identify cost-cutting opportunities and areas where it could work with artificial intelligence partners. 

To date, the company has already eliminated 3,000 contractors and employees under the plan, including by shaving its management layers, he said. He didn’t distinguish between contractors and workers.

“We've analyzed every non-core asset that we have,” Georgakopoulos said in answering an analyst’s question on the webcast. “We looked for assets that have either economic challenges or technology challenges or overlaps with other things that we do, or are not consistent with our long-term vision.” 

The company has talked with major banks about the sale of one of its debit networks, according to earlier reports, including by the Wall Street Journal.

Given those non-core assets are eating up capital and resources, the company has taken the approach that it needs to “rationalize,” or cut back in those areas for the benefit of the company’s long-term prospects, he explained. 

For the third-quarter, Fiserv reported a net loss of nearly $6 billion, including a significant noncash goodwill impairment of $6.45 billion related to its restructuring, as revenue slipped 1% to $5.2 billion, according to a Tuesday earnings press release.

Fiserv Chief Financial Officer Paul Todd referred to the cost-cutting plan as having $1 billion in “savings opportunities” during the webcast, saying on the webcast that some of the benefits wouldn’t start to show up until next year or later.

Fiserv has also begun having conversations with interested buyers for some parts of the business that aren’t central to its operations, he said.

“Through our portfolio review, we have identified a number of businesses and activities that are not core to our go-forward strategy and where we may pursue alternative ownership arrangements,” Georgakopoulos said on a webcast with analysts who follow the company. “We are in conversations with multiple parties, with [non-disclosure agreements] and processes in place, but it is too early to estimate the proceeds to Fiserv from these efforts.”

Georgakopoulos has been seeking to restructure the Milwaukee-based company since he was named CEO in June. He was appointed after the exit of Mike Lyons, who served in the post for only about one year after the exit last year of Frank Bisignano, who left to head the Social Security Administration.

Since Bisignano’s exit, the company has struggled with fallout from a lack of growth in its once high-growth Clover point-of-sale business. Shareholders have sued over that unit not satisfying past growth objectives.

One new way in which Georgakopoulos will now try to right the business is by selling Clover’s services to larger companies. He described Tuesday how in the past Clover, which is focused on small and midsize businesses, lost clients after they grew larger.

“This expansion enables Clover to go beyond small businesses to sell larger, more complex merchants with multiple locations, bridging a key gap in Clover's current offering,” Georgakopoulos said on the webcast.

title: FTC, states sue Toast over fees
snippet: The agency and eight states allege that the point-of-sale services provider charges its restaurant clients and their customers hidden fees.
fullText:
The Federal Trade Commission and eight states sued Toast on Thursday, alleging that the point-of-sale company misled restaurant clients and their customers with hidden fees and subscription plans that were difficult to cancel. 

The lawsuit also said that Toast failed to deliver the customer support help that it had pledged, and obscured a 99-cent fee Toast collected from consumers who placed online orders.

“Toast failed to honor a number of its promises and instead imposed hidden fees, unauthorized charges and subscription traps that drained the hard‑earned profits of businesses just trying to serve their customers,” the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection director, Christopher Mufarrige, said Thursday in a press release.

The FTC was joined in the lawsuit by California and attorneys general in seven states: Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Utah.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for Northern California, says that “at least tens of thousands of consumers have complained about these issues to the FTC, online, and directly to Toast.”

Toast said in a press release that it disagreed with the allegations “and will vigorously defend” itself against the claims.

“Toast has been cooperating fully with the FTC's review of this matter since mid-2025 and has engaged in good faith throughout, including efforts to reach a resolution short of litigation,” the company said. “The FTC disregarded the information we provided showing the extent to which our restaurant customers negotiate their contracts. We are prepared to defend our business and fight this unprecedented action through litigation.” 

Boston-based Toast sells hardware and software services, including payment processing, to help restaurants and other merchants handle their sales.

As part of their Toast agreements, restaurants must enroll in auto-renewing subscriptions, with an average cost of $900 monthly, according to the lawsuit. The monthly cost is determined by how many terminals and added services a business chooses to bundle into the subscription, the plaintiffs said.

“Toast customers frequently complain that they have been enrolled in and charged for Toast subscription add-ons without their consent,” the lawsuit says. 

Toast has “used false claims” to entice customers to enroll in subscription services, including an offer of free Toast products under some pricing plans, along with “24/7/365” customer support, according to the lawsuit.

“In fact, none of Toast’s hardware is $0, and Toast customers frequently claim that they cannot get customer support at any hour of the day,” the lawsuit said.

The company has also made it difficult for customers to end their subscriptions, according to the lawsuit.

“The convoluted, multi-step cancellation process instituted by Toast, combined with Toast’s customer support failures, prevents or makes it hard for consumers to cancel their subscriptions, saddling consumers with additional months or even years of unwanted charges,” the government plaintiffs wrote. 

The lawsuit said that Toast’s subscription cancellation process is “nonintuitive, time-consuming, far from simple, and requires the involvement and cooperation of multiple teams within Toast.”

For those who successfully ended their Toast accounts, “in many instances, Toast has hit them with unexpected high-dollar early termination fees or continued to charge them for subscription services without consent,” the lawsuit says.

The lawsuit also said that Toast is collecting obscured fees from restaurant patrons who order online.

Until July 2023, Toast collected a 99-cent fee from diners using online digital sales channels for orders above $10, beyond other fees it charged restaurants, according to the lawsuit. The company began testing this fee in some locations in September 2021, according to the lawsuit.

“Nowhere did Toast state that it, not local restaurants, would keep the fee,” the plaintiffs said. “Instead, Toast used language obscuring that it was the primary or sole beneficiary of the fee.”

The lawsuit alleges that Toast violated the FTC Act and the 2010 Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, along with the states’ consumer protection and unfair and deceptive trade practices laws.

In its press release, Toast said that no court has found that the ROSCA law applies to “negotiated business-to-business agreements, and we don’t believe it applies here.”

Toast is scheduled to report its third-quarter financial results on Tuesday.

Correction: This story has been updated to correct that Toast ended a 99-cent customer fee in July 2023.
